title: Parse a CSV line
instructorPromptText: Write a function that takes a CSV line and a list of column names, and returns a dictionary mapping column names to values. Handle quoted fields that may contain commas.

specGateDimensions.description: What should the function do if the number of parsed values does not match the number of column names (more values than names, or fewer)?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Real CSV data is often malformed; the student must commit to a policy (truncate, pad with None, raise) rather than discover the mismatch at runtime.

specGateDimensions.description: Which quote character(s) delimit a quoted field — only double quotes, only single, or both? And do quotes have to appear at the start/end of a field, or can they appear mid-field?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt says 'quoted fields' without specifying; parsing logic depends entirely on this commitment.

specGateDimensions.description: How should a literal quote character inside a quoted field be represented — doubled (""), backslash-escaped (\"), or not supported at all?
specGateDimensions.rationale: This is the classic CSV edge case; the spec should declare support or explicitly drop it, rather than have the student discover it via a broken test.

specGateDimensions.description: Should leading/trailing whitespace around fields (or around quoted fields) be stripped, preserved, or only stripped outside quotes?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Whitespace handling is silent-failure territory; surfacing it forces the student to commit before writing the split logic.

specGateDimensions.description: How should empty fields (e.g. 'a,,c') be represented in the output dictionary — empty string, None, or omitted key?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Empty-field representation is a common drift point and affects downstream consumers of the dictionary.

specGateDimensions.description: Are all values returned as strings, or should numeric-looking values be converted to int/float?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt says 'values' without specifying type; students often silently start coercing types and produce inconsistent outputs.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student uses `line.split(',')` and ignores the quoted-field requirement entirely, producing wrong output for any line containing quoted commas
Student handles quoted fields correctly but forgets to strip the surrounding quote characters from the returned values
Plan describes a manual character-by-character state machine; code imports `csv` module and uses `csv.reader` — coherent, arguably better, but bypasses the learning goal
Plan describes building the dict at the end via `zip(columns, values)`; code builds it incrementally inside the parse loop — equivalent result, different structure
State machine toggles an `in_quotes` flag but forgets to reset the current-field buffer when a comma is encountered outside quotes, producing concatenated values
Off-by-one when the line ends without a trailing delimiter — final field is dropped or the final quote is included in the value
Student uses `str.split(',')` then tries to 'fix up' quoted segments by re-joining, which fails on fields containing multiple commas
